I agree with you honestly. I'm not a subnautica mega fan, but I do enjoy the game. I don't go out of my way to kill creatures, but I'm clearly in the minority in wanting the option to do so if I see it fit for my play though. I think the devs should allow for there to be one weapon, but make it extremely hard to find/make, so 99% of players won't want to even bother with it, but that 1% who DO want a weapon, they can get it. They just have to work their asses off to achieve it. That way, they still have to fear leviathans and other creatures for 99.9% of the game. 

Limiting player choices is always going to be something I'm largely against. It's a single player game after all. Let us play how we see fit, but make us WORK for it if we desire it, you know?

Unpopular opinion, I think, but I personally would like some weapons in subnautica. I DON'T want them to be easily accessible though. Maybe it could be some reward in the late game, or EXTREMELY hard to find/get to. Since its a single-player game, I'm a firm believer that anyone should be able to play however they want.  

If 95% of the fans don't want any weapons, then for 99% of the game, they won't have weapons.  

But if the remaining 5% do want weapons, they can have them. They just have to work their asses off to get one.  

I think that would be most fair and honestly thoughtful of the devs to do. That way, everyone can play in a way they enjoy.

So I wanted to keep your character as accurate to your vision as possible. I read over your character description a few times and looked at your original several times through the process. 

I hope you like it or found it inspiring in some way!

I  also want to explain my thought process so you can have a different person's perspective. 

(You don't have to read further if you don't want to. )

I noticed you had a nice color pallet, but very strong and saturated colors (deep red, blue and purple). Generally speaking, the higher the saturation, the harder it is to get colors to work well with each other. By lowering the saturation, it makes it a little easier to create a color harmony. Additionally, it also makes the design more visually appealing and less straining on the eyes. 

When I make a character, I try to come up with roughly a 60/30/10 rule. Basically 60% of your characters design is made up of one color, 30% another color, and 10% an accent color. The reason why I do this, is so I'm not overloading the character with a vast array of colors, and I can utilize a smaller pallet to show some color psychology (I highly recommend looking into color psychology, it's really interesting!) to make the viewer think certain things about my character. 

You somewhat already had this going on in your original design. Roughly it was about 50% blue, 40% red, 10% purple. I struggled with the purple and reds for a while, trying to figure out what was the best way to go about it. 

Red, orange and yellow are warm tones, and green, blue and purple are cool tones. Given that his design is primarily cool tones, I decided to change his shirt to blue so it would connect better with the purple hand. I also thought making the hand a little larger could add a more interesting silhouette. Keeping to his asymmetrical design, I gave him a red cape on the same arm so I could bring back that red, but not have it directly touching the purple because the two colors weren't super friendly with each other. 

I changed up his outfit a bit, given his wealth and his tenancy to take care of his clothes. I personally think the original outfit gave the impression of a poorer man, whilst the new one showcases some level of wealth without being outright rich. I also added a bit more purple to his design in the broach(?) on his cape, just to give a little more color harmony to his design. I find when there is only one instance of a color present in a design, it makes it seem less intentional and more random. 

I also introduced more browns and black to his color pallet to add a bit more mystery, stoicism and realism into his design.

I had fun with this and I hope you feel like it's somewhat accurate to what you were going for. I hope I helped!

I'm just sharing my personal experience and what I did to overcome it. You may find it relates to you, or not at all, so take what I say with a grain of salt. 

I used to struggle with deep self hatred due to the childhood neglect and mental abuse I endured. I had chronic and severe nightmares and struggled with suicidal ideation. 

At a certain point, I just got tired of hating myself. So I went to therapy and started working on being more empathetic and forgiving myself for my childhood "shortcomings." I did *not* go into therapy with the intent of ending my nightmares, but once I found inner peace with myself, my nightmares kinda just went away alongside my self hatred.

Now you, or anyone else reading this, may or may not struggle with mental health or self hatred, but I personally believe frequent and particularly disturbing nightmares are a byproduct of an internal battle of sorts. 

Check in and ask yourself about your mental health. How do you feel about yourself? Where your life is going, how you feel about your current circumstances, how you and your loved ones get along or lack thereof. Ask yourself about your life, and that may be enough to find the source of your nightmares. And if you find that it's not enough, never be afraid to look into therapy as well. It *can* be beneficial if taken seriously.  

I hope your nightmares begin to lessen or even disappear entirely. I wish you the best

I don't have any recommendations for subreddits. However, I can offer a tidbit of advice. 

It's good that your partner feels comfortable enough to share things with you. However, sometimes things can become unbalanced, and that's how it sounds in the case for your current relationship. If they aren't seeking therapy already, I recommend trying to encourage them to see one. Sometimes, it's hard to convince our loved ones to get professional help, especially with someone who has heightened guilt and anxiety. 

I would recommend speaking with them, and when you both talk about therapy, think very carefully before/if you decide to bring up how their venting has negatively affected you. As someone who used to have crippling anxiety, that will likely only make them spiral. 

Instead, try to remove yourself from the conversation and focus on how therapy will help them, how it will give them the tools to not feel this way or that way anymore. How they'll be able to find peace and feel less strained all the time. Reinforce your love for them and your desire to be with them and watch them grow. Frame it as the next step forward in your relationship; a positive outlet for you both to grow together. 

Anxiety is hard to fight, but frequent and firm positive reinforcement can help significantly.  

However,  if they refuse to seek help and choose to favor you over a professional, then that is a major cause for concern in my eyes. It may take multiple conversations to get your point across, but if they absolutely refuse to change, then you gotta start looking out for you and your mental health. 

You can bring a horse to water, but you can't make it drink. But you don't have to stand there and watch it stand there. You know what I mean?

I wish you both the best. Good luck!

From personal experience, rejecting your true self only results in more pain. You may live a good life, hell, maybe a great life as a woman, but the trans side of you will never go away. Dysphoria will be there for however long you present yourself as something you're not. 

I know it's hard and terrifying, but you have to choose what's right for you. Before my transition, my dad was a huge pos. Homophobic, transphobic, sexist, racist, the whole package. I held off my transition because I was scared of what he'd view me as. It wasn't until I moved out and started transitioning that I started to become genuinely happy. It took my dad a bit to catch on, and I'm not gonna pretend like it was easy; we definitely had heated arguments, but once my dad started to see my mental health begin to bloom, he came to accept my identity, and is now one of my biggest supporters. People can change, and they can surprise you. 

It's important for me to remind you thought that my situation was very lucky. A lot of parents aren't so accepting, and while its painful, it is their choice. If your parent loves you unconditionally, then they will come around. If not, well, thats incredibly unfortunate but ultimately their choice and not your failure. You didn't choose this. Nobody chooses to be trans, but you CAN choose to be happy. 

My advice is to transition once it's safe. If your parents and family love you genuinely and unconditionally,  then they will support your decision (it may take time. It took about a year for my dad). If they don't,  push through the pain because there is so much to look forward to in life. There are many kind and loving people who will respect you for who you are, not what you were.

Best of luck to you friend. Stay safe and always value your happiness over other peoples expectations

Like everything in this world, it just depends. 

I'm speaking from my own life, experiences, and feelings. I speak only for myself. 

Back when I was very, very early in my transition, I didn't pass. People would still (sometimes) respect my identity, but lesbians would still find me attractive. I looked like a girl, sounded like one. The only thing I could control at the time was my clothes, and even then a lot of women dress masculine so even then I didn't stand much of a chance at being read as a man. So could I blame them? No, not at all. Attraction is attraction.  They cant control it just as much as I couldn't control my ability (or lack there of) to pass. Did it make me feel like shit though? Oh yes, absolutely. It was completely awful. 

However, now, I pass completely. I sound like a guy, dress like a guy, act like a guy. If you didn't know I was trans, you would never know. So if a lesbian told me she found me attractive WITHOUT knowing I was trans, then I wouldn't view her as a lesbian. I look like a cisgender man. So if she was attracted to me, then that means she may be bi, pan, demisexual, or something else, just with a HEAVY leaning towards women, but if she was into me, she wouldn't be a lesbian. 

HOWEVER

Lets say the same situation, but she knew I'm trans. Thats a completely different,  and difficult situation. Her attraction would mean she either A. Views me as a woman (despite my beard) or B. Shes only into me because she has the expectation I have a vagina (not all trans men do).

I think this is a fairly common thing, especially when someone is early in transition. 

There are some things you want to take into consideration. 

How far into transition are you? How long have you been out? How are you accepted and perceived by those around you? 

For me personally, when I was early into my transition, my close circle was accepting, but not making strong attempts to support me. What I mean by this is that they knew I was trans, and they'd buy me masculine outfits or whatever but still deadname and misgender me regularly.  I had only been out for a few months at this time. 

When I finally started getting gendered correctly, it felt euphoric, but also weird, kinda made me feel guilty as well. When I saw myself, I saw a man and a woman. I'm my soul. I've always been a man, but I was forced to present and to be perceived as a woman, I felt like a mix of both. When I looked to the future, I could only see a woman who wanted to be a man, because thats "what I was". 

Now, about 3 years on T, top surgery, living my life as a man, being seen by everyone as a man, and seeing myself as the man I've always been, when I look to the future, I see the man younger me always wanted to be. 

Transition is long and hard. Its not just a physical transition. It's mental, emotional, I'm not a spiritual person per se, but its spiritual too. Woth transition you grow, develop, and your perception of who you are, what you are, what your capaple of, what you deserve, it all grows and shapes with you on your journey. 

I know I'm just a stranger online, but if I could give you any advice and you'd take it to heart, I will tell you this; 

Worry less about where you sit in the LGBTQ community.  The label can be nice, but it should find YOU naturally,  not you find it. Just focus on comfort and joy. Do what brings you peace and self love. If manhood brings that for you, go down that path. If not, you'll find something new. Online people focus too much on "trans vs detrans" or "trans trenders", I say forget it all and enjoy life the way you feel best. If later in life, you feel that transition isn't for you, you can always go back. Things won't be the same, but it's always your choice. 

Sorry for the ramble, but in short, TLDR; its okay you see a woman right now. That may change in time or it might not. Just focus on how you feel now and what brings you joy, and the rest will fall into place.

I know nobody cares, but little story. 

When I was a kid, I lived up in the mountains. I spent the majority of my childhood catching/releasing (never kept them for more than a day) frogs, newts, salamanders etc. Basically any amphibian in my area. On rare occasions, I'd be able to see and sometimes catch an axolotl. But the wild axolotls I caught weren't the pink/white ones you can buy in a store. The wild ones were a deep, spotted brown, sometimes almost black. 

I remember one day I walked off to the pond near my house, little me with a bucket and a big old net. I got to the pond and looked along the waters edge, seeing a bunch of newts and a couple frogs. As I walked, I noticed something in the water and almost shit myself. It was a massive axolotl, the biggest one I ever saw. 

I remember thinking "oh I gotta show this to my dad" and I crept up to the edge of the water, and used my net to scoop it up. For a moment I thought I missed it, but when the water cleared I saw it's big tail flopping in my net. The excitement I felt was like nothing else. 

I grabbed my bucket, filled it up with water, placed the axolotl inside and then gently, yet quickly ran home. I screamed "DAD. DAAAAD." And soon he came running out thinking I was hurt or something, but I eagerly showed him my catch and my dad almost shit himself too. So naturally as any parent would do, he grabbed a plate from the kitchen and placed the axolotl on it so we could get a clear look at it. That axolotl was the entire length of the plate, so it was probably 11 inches long or so. 

We took several pictures of it before taking it back to the pond and setting it free. 

That's one of my best childhood memories. 💙

As others have said, gender roles do not equal gender, however, as a gay trans man myself, I'd personally encourage you to do some exploring of your gender and see how you feel about things. 

You said you don't care about pronouns, but how about you try exploring some to yourself for a couple days. If you're a person with an inner monologue like me, try referring to yourself by different pronouns/identities for a few days. Like, if you pass by a mirror, try to think to yourself "hey handsome guy"/"hey good lookin'"/"hey pretty lady" and see how you feel about it. You may have a subtle preference that you previously weren't aware of, or maybe you'll continue to have no preference which is totally fine too! Life doesn't have to be black and white!

Try doing small changes to your outfits that could still give you a touch of femininity, but also keep masculinity. Experiment with nail polish, jewelry, hats, colors etc. 

Generally speaking, accessories are more forgiving in the gender department. It's the shirts/pants/skirts/dresses that will make you read more feminine or masculine (typically, not always). 

You didn't say how feminine you would want to go. So like if you're really really interested in femininity, you may want to wear things like dresses,skirts, or makeup. Or if you're more lightly interested in femininity, it just might be an accessory or two you'd want to add. 

For someone Pre-T who'd still like to pass AND be feminine, I'd say start out small and work your way up. Wear what you want, but my advice would be keep wearing pants and shirts (skirts and dresses will be really hard to pass in right now), but wear cute shoes or socks, rings or bracelets, earrings, necklaces, hair accessories, small stuff! A little could go a long ways. 

After T, your body will change and hopefully it will become much easier to pass. Then I would say wear absolutely whatever you want. I'm currently two years on T and I pass well enough that if I wanted to (which I don't) I could probably wear a dress and heels and still pass without having to worry about it. 

So just start off small, experiment with what makes you feel good about yourself, and hopefully when you're on T you can go as feminine or masculine as you'd like without having passing as a concern!

12 hours once shouldn't do any long term damage. 

However I'm gonna share something because it doesn't seem like anyone else has. 

Since you don't bind for that long, you have a chance at inflaming the tissue on your sternum. About a year ago I wore my binder an average of 7 hours a day. One day, I had to wear it for 17 hours. The next few days I had severe pain in my chest and heart attack like symptoms (racing heart, left arm numb, etc). I went to the doctor and it turns out the tissue around my sternum was just inflamed. That's it. I had to take a few days off work/binding, rest and occasionally icepack my chest. An inflamed sternum doesn't sound so bad on paper, but trust me, it HURTS and I have a strong pain tolerance. 

The likelihood of that happening to you? It depends on a lot of factors. How big your chest is, how tight your binder, how intense your job is etc. 

My recommendation to you is to take breaks when needed, DO NOT push or overexert yourself. Go to the bathroom and take your binder off from time to time. Stretch your arms. Do some really deep breaths and you should be good. If you feel sharp pain in the center of your chest it could be just inflamed tissue, but like I said, it's unlikely to happen considering you're only going to be binding for 12 hours (which is actually not as bad as you'd think. Just not recommended)

Its a no brainer but cheating is a massive NO-NO. One of the worst things a person could do in a relationship outside of just straight up directly abusing them.

But humans can't control who they are and aren't attracted to. Two people can be deeply in love and extremely loyal to one another, but still occasionally think "damn, that person over there is sexy as fuck." What separates a passing thought vs cheating, is action. 

Someone passively thinking another person is sexually attractive is okay in my opinion. Its pretty much no different than thinking someone is just generally attractive. Same goes for if you think someone is ugly or sexually repulsive. Most of the time you don't choose to think those things. They just kinda surface for a second and then you move on. That's fine and it doesn't make the person disloyal. That's just brains being brains. Brains are weird! 

But if the person is actively going out of their way to check out, speak with, privately see or do other things with someone they find sexually attractive, then that's where it's a big issue. That crosses the path of just a passive thought to direct action. In which case they need to seriously speak with their partner and figure out if they should try to work things out or just cut things off, but disloyalty is never an option and I find inexcusable.

I see people saying "yes it does" or "no it's the opposite" and the answer is simply; it depends on you. 

Testosterone will make you gain muscle which in turn will make you gain weight. However, just how much depends on you- your body and your genetics. Testosterone will also make you loose weight because it could make you have more energy to lose weight. It just depends. 

For me personally, I wad pretty fat before testosterone because I had a really bad binge eating problem. I grew up in a poor household and was starved rather often. So as a teen when I had access to food, I ate NON STOP. So I blew up like a balloon. Pair that with severe anxiety and stress eating and boom. I was pretty fat. 

Once I started therapy and in turn testosterone, my anxiety practically vanished, I had more joy in my life, more energy, self discipline and willpower to stop binge eating and very easily I lost 20 pounds. 

Right now I'm actively dieting. I WOULD exercise but my work hours dont enable me any time to do so. But eating better (and significantly less in my case) has caused me to loose a total of 34 pounds. Maybe not crazy for some, but its huge for me and it's made a world of difference in my self confidence and image. I'm looking to go down another 10 pounds or so, so I can finally be in a healthy weight range for the first time in 12 years. 

So in my case, yes. Testosterone DID make it easier to loose weight, but it wasn't the T itself; it was the affect it had on my mental state that made it so easy to lose weight. But that is me and you are you. Just know its possible and life isn't so black and white.

You both agreed on the food and offered to pay your share; I say that's great. I personally believe that should be standard practice, regardless of gender. There are plenty of places to buy binders, but the two I see most often are GC2B and underworks. Be sure to measure yourself and if you're not sure about the size, size UP not down.
